title: Validating Input and Reporting Errors
summary: Check every request at the edge, decide between 400, 409, and 422, and answer every error in one Problem Details format.
intro: Everything a client sends is just text, and some of it is wrong: a typo, a phone app two versions behind, a script written in a hurry, and now and then a person poking for weaknesses. An API that trusts what arrives ends up storing a booking for minus five people, crashing on a date it can't read, or answering with an error so vague nobody can fix their request. This lesson shows you how to check every request where it enters, with a schema for each body and query string, where each kind of check belongs, and which status code each failure earns. Then it gives every error one shape, the Problem Details format, built in one central place in Express.

steps.title: Never trust input
steps.body:
Your server can't see who is on the other end. A request from Roombook's own web app looks just like one typed into curl, and anyone can type into curl. So every part of a request, its path, query string, headers, and body, is input from outside, and could be anything at all. It goes wrong in two ways:

- **Wrong by mistake**: a misspelled field, a date in the wrong format, a number sent as text, an end time before the start, or a client built against last year's version of the API.
- **Hostile on purpose**: a fifty-megabyte body, a note of a million characters, an id of `-1` or `99999999999999999999`, or a field nobody should be able to set, like `"isAdmin": true`, or `"status": "confirmed"` on a booking that broke the rules.

## Parse at the edge

The answer is to check everything in one place: the **edge** of your API, where requests come in, before any of your own code uses them. Picture a line drawn around your server's code, called the **trust boundary**. Outside the line is text from strangers. Inside are values your code can rely on.

```diagram validation-and-errors-trust
Text from outside is checked once, at the boundary, and only typed values go further in.
```

Crossing the line is the job of **parsing**: turning text into typed values, or refusing. A parser for a booking doesn't just answer yes or no. It hands back a booking whose `attendees` is a whole number from 1 to 30, whose times are real moments in UTC, and which has no fields nobody expected. Code inside the line takes that value and never checks those things again. The idea has a slogan: **parse, don't validate**. Checking the text and then passing the text on leaves every later function wondering whether it was checked. Passing on the parsed value makes the checking part of the type.

A **schema** is how you describe a valid input: each field, its type, whether it's required, and its limits. A schema library reads a request against it and gives back either the typed value or a list of everything that's wrong.

## Why TypeScript's types don't do this

TypeScript's types exist only while you write and check your code. Node strips them before it runs anything, so at run time there's no type left to check `req.body` against. `req.body` is typed `any`, and writing `const input: CreateBooking = req.body` is a promise you make to the compiler, not a check. Whatever JSON arrived is what you get, as the example shows with a handler that writes `req.body` straight back.

That's why Roombook uses **zod**, a schema library for TypeScript. A zod schema checks real values at run time, and TypeScript can work out the parsed value's type from the schema, so you write each shape once and get both the check and the type.

examples.title: A handler that trusts its input
examples.prompt: This handler, from before this lesson, answers `201` with `{ id: 1001, ...req.body }`. Send it nonsense.
examples.explanation: Every field came back exactly as sent, and the handler answered 201 Created. The room id is a name, the start time is the word `whenever`, there are minus five people, and the client has quietly made itself an admin. TypeScript had nothing to say, because by the time this ran, TypeScript was gone. A real handler would now store this, and the bug would surface later, far from its cause: a crash when some code calls `.getTime()` on `whenever`, or a page listing a booking for minus five people. The fix isn't more care in each handler. It's a schema at the edge, so this request never gets past the first line.

steps.title: Schemas for request bodies
steps.body:
A booking request says which room, when it starts and ends, and how many people are coming, with an optional note. Here is everything its schema checks, and why:

- **Required fields and types**: `roomId` and `attendees` are whole numbers, `startsAt` and `endsAt` are times, and `note` is text or absent.
- **Formats**: times are written in **RFC 3339**, the standard text form of a date and time that JSON APIs use, like `2026-10-05T14:00:00Z` or `2026-10-05T16:00:00+02:00`. A time without an offset from UTC is refused, since `14:00` alone means a different moment in every time zone.
- **Ranges and lengths**: `roomId` is positive, `attendees` is 1 to 30, the most any room holds, and `note` is at most 500 characters. Limits like these protect the server as much as the data. A note with no limit invites someone to store a megabyte of text in every booking.
- **No unknown fields.** A client that sends `notes` instead of `note` learns about its typo at once, instead of wondering why the note never saved. A client that tries to set `status` or `userId` itself is told no, instead of having its field quietly kept, or quietly dropped.
- **Rules across fields**: `endsAt` must be after `startsAt`. That needs nothing but the request itself, so the schema can check it.

## Normalize on the way in

Parsing can also tidy what it accepts, so the rest of the code only ever sees one form of each value. This is called **normalizing**. Roombook trims spaces from the ends of the note, and converts both times to UTC, so `16:00+02:00` and `14:00Z` become the same moment. From the authentication lesson on, emails are lowercased the same way.

Here is the create schema, in `src/modules/bookings/bookings.schemas.ts`:

```ts
import { z } from "zod";

const Instant = z.iso.datetime({ offset: true }).transform((s) => new Date(s));

export const CreateBookingBody = z
  .strictObject({
    roomId: z.int().positive(),
    startsAt: Instant,
    endsAt: Instant,
    attendees: z.int().min(1).max(30),
    note: z.string().trim().max(500).optional(),
  })
  .refine((b) => b.endsAt > b.startsAt, { path: ["endsAt"], message: "must be after startsAt" });

export type CreateBookingInput = z.infer<typeof CreateBookingBody>;
```

- `z.strictObject` refuses any key the schema doesn't list. A plain `z.object` would quietly drop them instead.
- `z.int()` accepts only whole numbers, so `"1"` and `2.5` are both refused.
- `z.iso.datetime({ offset: true })` accepts RFC 3339 times with `Z` or an offset like `+02:00`, and `.transform()` turns the text into a `Date`, which is always a moment in UTC.
- `.trim()` normalizes the note before `.max(500)` measures it.
- `.refine()` adds the rule across two fields, reported on `endsAt`. zod runs it only once every field is valid on its own, since it can't compare a time that didn't parse.

`z.infer` gives you the parsed type for free: `CreateBookingInput` has `startsAt: Date`, not `string`. The controller parses with it in one line, `const input = CreateBookingBody.parse(req.body)`. `.parse()` throws a `ZodError` listing every problem when the body doesn't fit, and part 6 turns that error into a response.

## One schema per operation

Creating, replacing, and changing part of a booking need different schemas, even though they describe the same thing. A create requires `roomId`. A PATCH, the method from the routes lesson for changing part of a resource, can't move a booking to another room, so it has no `roomId` at all, and every field it does have is optional. Reusing the create schema for PATCH would demand fields the client didn't mean to change, and would let it send ones it mustn't. A PATCH also has to tell a field that's missing, which means leave it alone, from one sent as `null`, which means clear it, as the routes lesson explained.

Here is the PATCH schema, in the same file. `.partial()` makes every field optional, so a missing field stays `undefined`, and `.nullable()` lets the note alone also be `null`, which clears it:

```ts
export const UpdateBookingBody = z
  .strictObject({
    startsAt: Instant,
    endsAt: Instant,
    attendees: z.int().min(1).max(30),
    note: z.string().trim().max(500).nullable(),
  })
  .partial()
  .refine((b) => !b.startsAt || !b.endsAt || b.endsAt > b.startsAt, {
    path: ["endsAt"],
    message: "must be after startsAt",
  });
```

examples.title: Normalized on the way in
examples.prompt: Book Turing with a start time two hours ahead of UTC, and a note with spaces around it.
examples.code: curl -s localhost:4000/v1/bookings -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"roomId": 1, "startsAt": "2026-10-05T16:00:00+02:00", "endsAt": "2026-10-05T15:30:00Z", "attendees": 3, "note": "  Algorithms study group  "}'
examples.explanation: The request said `16:00:00+02:00`, and the stored booking says `14:00:00Z`: the same moment, now in UTC, so every later comparison, like checking for overlaps, compares like with like. The spaces around the note are gone. The rest of the booking comes from the service and the store, which the next lesson builds: an id, the user, a status, a version, and when it was created, which is the course's fixed clock. None of those were the client's to set, and the schema made sure they weren't.

examples.title: Several mistakes, one answer
examples.prompt: Send a booking with several things wrong at once.
examples.output: {"type":"https://roombook.example/problems/validation-failed","title":"Validation failed","status":422,"detail":"4 fields are invalid.","instance":"/v1/bookings","requestId":"3dfce0f8-373f-4369-9445-46881735bb02","errors":[{"field":"roomId","message":"Invalid input: expected number, received string"},{"field":"startsAt","message":"Invalid ISO datetime"},{"field":"attendees","message":"Too small: expected number to be >=1"},{"field":"notes","message":"is not a known field"}]}
examples.explanation: One answer lists all four problems: the room id was text, the start time wasn't a time, there were zero attendees, and `notes` isn't a field. The messages are zod's own, and `field` names the key in the body, so a web app can put each message next to the right input. The rule that `endsAt` comes after `startsAt` didn't run, since `startsAt` never parsed. The shape of the whole answer, with `type`, `title`, and the rest, is part 5's subject.

steps.title: Path, query, and header values

examples.title: A query string with three mistakes
examples.prompt: Ask for rooms with a capacity that isn't a number, a limit over the maximum, and a made-up cursor.
examples.output: {"type":"https://roombook.example/problems/validation-failed","title":"Validation failed","status":422,"detail":"3 fields are invalid.","instance":"/v1/rooms","requestId":"4383db19-89b3-4eaf-92c7-8f635ac5f8b3","errors":[{"field":"minCapacity","message":"must be a whole number"},{"field":"limit","message":"Too big: expected number to be <=100"},{"field":"cursor","message":"is not a cursor this API issued"}]}
examples.explanation: All three problems come back at once: `lots` isn't a whole number, `500` is over the limit, and `abc` isn't a cursor the API made. `instance` is the path without the query string. The answer is the same shape as the body errors in part 2, so a client handles both with the same code. Ask for `minCapacity=5&limit=1` instead, and you get Turing alone, with a `nextCursor` for the next page.

examples.title: An id that names nothing
examples.prompt: Ask for a booking whose id isn't a number.
examples.explanation: A path that can't name a booking is a 404, the same answer as a booking id that's a number but doesn't exist. To the client, both mean there's nothing at that URL, so there's no reason to tell them apart, and no reason to say how ids are checked. The `type` is Roombook's `not-found` problem, the same for every 404.

steps.title: Where each check belongs

examples.title: Three broken rules
examples.prompt: Book Lovelace, which holds four, for five people, starting at a quarter past and lasting three and three quarter hours.
examples.output: {"type":"https://roombook.example/problems/validation-failed","title":"Validation failed","status":422,"detail":"3 fields are invalid.","instance":"/v1/bookings","requestId":"b6f4bd88-dac6-42b1-97e9-7628090e12a9","errors":[{"field":"startsAt","message":"must be on the hour or half past"},{"field":"endsAt","message":"a booking lasts 30 minutes to 3 hours"},{"field":"attendees","message":"Lovelace holds at most 4 people"}]}
examples.explanation: The body passed the schema: every field had the right type and range. Then the service found three broken rules and reported all of them, in the same shape as the schema's errors: the start isn't on the hour or half past, the booking is longer than three hours, and Lovelace holds four. It's a 422, since this request is wrong no matter what anyone else has booked. Only the request can be fixed, and the messages say exactly what to change.

examples.title: A booking that clashes
examples.prompt: With Ada's 14:00 to 15:30 booking of Turing already made, book Turing from 15:00 to 16:00.
examples.output: {"type":"https://roombook.example/problems/booking-overlap","title":"Room already booked","status":409,"detail":"The room is already booked then.","instance":"/v1/bookings","requestId":"6e1aa083-8b53-47f1-87a8-72c55a22ab3e"}
examples.explanation: Every field and every rule was fine, so the request reached the store, which found the overlap with the existing booking and refused. It's a 409, with its own type, `booking-overlap`, so a client can tell it apart from every other conflict and offer to show the room's free times. The same request succeeds once the other booking is cancelled, which is what makes it a conflict and not a 422. Once the lesson on constraints and transactions moves the check into the database, the answer stays exactly the same.

steps.title: One error format: Problem Details

examples.title: A problem, headers and all
examples.prompt: Ask for a booking that doesn't exist, and look at the headers as well as the body.
examples.explanation: The headers say what the body is before a client reads a byte of it: `application/problem+json`. Express adds `charset=utf-8`, which is fine. The body has the five standard members, with `not-found` as the type, the same one every 404 in Roombook uses, and the detail saying which booking. `requestId` matches the `X-Request-Id` header, so whoever reports the error can quote it. The `grep` kept the status line, the content type, and the body.

steps.title: Central error handling

examples.title: Broken JSON
examples.prompt: Send a body that stops halfway through.
examples.output: {"type":"https://roombook.example/problems/invalid-json","title":"Body is not valid JSON","status":400,"detail":"The body couldn't be parsed as JSON.","instance":"/v1/bookings","requestId":"fa58978a-cb36-4f91-96e7-2d0ac4a31313"}
examples.explanation: `express.json()` couldn't parse the body and raised an error with `type: "entity.parse.failed"`, which `toProblem` turned into the `invalid-json` problem. It's a 400, not a 422, because there's no content to judge: the server couldn't read the request at all. The detail doesn't repeat the parser's own message, which can quote parts of the body back.

examples.title: A crash, answered safely
examples.prompt: Ask for a test route whose handler fails with `connection to the database was lost`.
examples.output: {"type":"https://roombook.example/problems/internal-error","title":"Internal server error","status":500,"detail":"Something went wrong on our side. Quote the request id if you report it.","instance":"/v1/crash","requestId":"831f33b4-aa69-4bd6-9fc5-376e395dac64"}
examples.explanation: The client gets the generic `internal-error` problem and the request id, and not a word about the database. The server's terminal has the rest: one JSON line with `"level":"error"`, the same request id, the message, and the stack trace. Anyone who reports the error can quote the id, and whoever fixes it can find that line in seconds.

examples.title: A body over the limit
examples.prompt: Send a 200 KB body: `big.json` holds a note of 200,000 letters.
examples.output: {"type":"https://roombook.example/problems/body-too-large","title":"Request body too large","status":413,"detail":"The body is larger than 100 KB.","instance":"/v1/bookings","requestId":"2cf9b40d-8c7d-47d6-b98d-1959e90459e9"}
examples.explanation: `express.json({ limit: "100kb" })` stopped reading at the limit and raised `entity.too.large`, which became the `body-too-large` problem, a 413. The note never reached the schema, whose own limit is 500 characters, so the server never held more than 100 KB of it. The two limits do different jobs: the body limit protects the server's memory, and the schema's limit protects the data.

recap:
- Every part of a request is untrusted text, so parse it at the edge into typed values, and pass only those inward.
- TypeScript's types vanish when the code runs, so zod checks what actually arrives.
- A schema checks types, formats, ranges, and lengths, refuses unknown fields, and normalizes values, like times to UTC.
- Each operation gets its own schema, since create, replace, and patch need different fields.
- Query and path values are text too: convert them, give them defaults, and bound anything that costs the server work.
- Shape is checked at the edge, business rules in the service, and races in the database.
- 400 means unreadable, 422 means readable but invalid, and 409 means valid but in conflict with current data.
- Every error is a Problem Details object with a stable type, built in one central handler, and a 500 never reveals internals.
